question: GitHub issue #1: long agent sessions close to the commit limit logged 'non-consecutive token position' - a batch fed the recurrent state positions it had seen already (143363 after 143362 with 1260 new tokens), or skipped some (151599 after 143363 with 8192) - and ended in a GPU fault. What lets a slot's tokens and its memory come apart, and how is it kept from happening?

reproduction.agent_workload: tmp/kvr/agent_probe.py: tool definitions (~10K tokens of system prompt), tool results of 0.5-7K tokens, streamed answers, and between requests what agent clients do - regenerate, abort a stream part way, trim an old tool result, retry after an abort - on two conversations sharing one slot (and three on four slots), MTP on, the disk tier on. 0.1.13, one slot, 50 turns to 102K tokens: no warning. Without memory pressure nothing went wrong, which is what pointed at the error paths
reproduction.fault_injection: STRIX_FAULT=<site>:<n> throws std::bad_alloc - what an exhausted commit limit throws from anything that allocates - on the n-th pass through a site (tmp/kvr/fault_probe.py, an 18.6K-token prompt, then a retry and a continuation). At the first checkpoint of a prompt (ckpt:1) the per-slot handler caught it, released the slot and kept its conversation - with its tokens for a batch that never ran - and, the slot's tokens being left in a batch no slot owned, the server aborted on GGML_ASSERT(batch.slot_batched || batch.size() == 0). With other slots in the batch it would have run on: the next request for the conversation would have started past positions its memory never held, the 'skipped' warning. An exception in decode or post-decode released every slot the same way, their conversations kept

cause: every place the server catches an exception mid-turn - the per-slot handler, and the ones around pre-decode, decode and post-decode - released the slot and kept its conversation, although part of a batch had been recorded in its tokens and not run, or run and not recorded. Only the decode error codes cleared it ('it's complicated to keep track of how much of the current batch has been processed'). Under commit exhaustion those exceptions come from ordinary work - a checkpoint's 110 MB, a compute buffer - and once a conversation's recurrent state and tokens disagree, checkpoints made from it carry the disagreement on

fix.apply_slot_state_guard: a slot that throws leaves the batch being built and loses its conversation, as a decode error already made it; so does every slot an exception in pre-decode, decode or post-decode catches. Before a prompt batch the slot's tokens must match its memory - positions up to the next one, the recurrent state at the last one (for the hybrid memory: the highest position is the lower of the two caches', the lowest the recurrent one) - or the prompt is processed from its start, with a warning that names both. STRIX_FAULT is the test hook
fix.checked: all three fault sites now answer the failed request with an error and go on: the retry is processed from its first token, bitwise the tokens and probabilities of a server that never failed (the retry's last token was drafted in one run and decoded in the other - a draft-acceptance difference, the tokens the same). Agent workload on the fixed build, one slot and two conversations to 132K and 124K tokens over 80 turns, and four slots with three conversations to 98K tokens over 70 turns (eight re-layouts and evictions among them): no warning of either kind, so the check has no false positive there

checkpoints.question_from_the_user: a resident conversation keeps up to 32 checkpoints of 0.11 GB in system RAM - are the older ones needed at all?
checkpoints.what_uses_them: continuing a conversation needs none; a regenerate and the next turn of a template that drops the thinking go back to just before the last prompt's end, an edited last message to its start - the last prompt's checkpoints. Older ones only serve a deeper rewind (an edited earlier message, an agent trimming old tool output); without one the conversation is processed again from the nearest earlier checkpoint
checkpoints.resident: the manager passes --ctx-checkpoints 8 --checkpoint-min-step 32768: the last prompt's checkpoints and one per 32K tokens before them, at most 0.9 GB a slot instead of 3.5, and a deeper rewind replays at most ~32K tokens before the point it changes. Nothing is written for them while the conversation is resident
checkpoints.leaving: apply_disk_ckpt_step: a leaving conversation's older checkpoints go to the disk tier too, one every 32768 tokens, each written once (0.11 GB per 32K tokens of conversation, against 0.9 GB of rows). Before it a conversation read back from disk had only its last prompt's: an agent trimming an early tool result then processed it again from its first token (67.8K tokens, 79 s); with them it went back to its earliest checkpoint. In the agent run restores brought 6-8 checkpoints each

not_done: one slot, two conversations sharing more than half of the cached one (a long shared system prompt early in both): upstream reuses the slot in place without saving the other - it is processed again from the shared prefix when it returns
with MTP, a long answer after a checkpoint rewind can part from the first pass at a near tie (docs/results/disk-tier-v3-20260924.json, rewind)
